newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's PM wants new tax to help armed forces.
newsitem.headline: Russia's PM wants new tax to help armed forces.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin proposed a new tax on Tuesday to help Russia's cash-strapped armed forces, but gave no details of how the plan could work.
Speaking at the Federation Council upper house of parliament, Chernomyrdin said the proposed levy would help fund the sector's large arrears. But nothing had been agreed yet.
"The government is taking measures to stabilise the situation," Chernomyrdin said.
"A government commission on funding national defence, law enforcement activities and state security is being set up and a schedule of payment of military arrears is being prepared."
Chernomyrdin said special laws would have to be approved before any new tax to fund the military could be introduced.
Chernomyrdin's proposal was clearly aimed at resolving the military's huge cash problems without damaging government monetary policy. But its effectiveness is questionable.
Tax collection is a huge problem in Russia where tax evasion is a national sport.

The State Tax Service said on Tuesday that tax revenues fell almost 30 percent in September from August and were less than half the levels envisaged in the budget. Taxes were only 75 percent of budgeted levels in the first nine months.
But Chernomyrdin's proposal highlighted the sensitivity of the problem for a country where people with the guns traditionally play an important role.

Last month, Russia's military, led by security chief Alexander Lebed and Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, issued a series of grave warnings about the plight of the armed forces. Lebed has said the army is close to mutiny.
Many soldiers in the once-proud Russian army have not been paid for months and its facilities are neglected and run-down.
The army owes money to suppliers, including electricity firms which have more than once threatened to cut off power supplies to military bases.
The campaign by Lebed and Rodionov appeared to be a success and Yeltsin, who is preparing for heart surgery, said last week he was taking this issue under special control.
"Russia must have a modern and professional army. Serving in it must be a source of respect and prestige," he said.
Yeltsin promised during this year's election campaign to end conscription by 2000 and to create a new, professional army geared to the post-Cold War world.
He urged the new Russian Defence Council, which groups ministers and security officials and held its first meeting last week, to come up with concrete proposals to resolve the crisis.
The Kremlin press service said Chernomyrdin reported the Councils's recommendations to President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday.
The proposals included granting a fixed level of funding for the armed forces and military research and allocating finance to pay for military reform and reducing the size of the army.
